episteme.definition: Unqualified scientific knowledge obtained when we know the necessary cause (aitia) through which a fact holds and see that it cannot be otherwise.

apodeixis.definition: A syllogism productive of scientific knowledge (syllogismos epistēmonikos), proceeding from premisses that are true, primary, immediate, better known than, prior to, and causes of the conclusion.

nous.loci: Anal. Post. II.19, 100b5–17; De Anima III.4–5, 429a10–430a25
nous.definition: The supreme noetic state (hexis) that apprehends immediate, indemonstrable first principles; more exact and truer than epistēmē itself, serving as the principle of principle (archē archēs).

epagoge.definition: Not probabilistic enumeration, but the genetic process by which sense-perception and memory bring the universal nature to a stand in the soul until nous intuits the necessary connection.

axioma.definition: An immediate principle that anyone who is going to learn anything must grasp of himself—prototypically the quantitative axiom 'if equals be subtracted from equals, the remainders are equal' (Euclid C.N. 3).

aitema.definition: A demonstrable or constructive assumption adopted without the learner's prior conviction or contrary to the learner's opinion; precursor to Euclid's five geometrical Postulates.

hypothesis.loci: Anal. Post. I.2, 72a18–24; I.10, 76b3–39; Topics VIII.3, 158b30
hypothesis.definition: A thesis asserting the existence (to einai) of the primitive objects of a science's genus—such as units in arithmetic or points and lines in geometry—from which attributes are demonstrated.

horismos.definition: A thesis stating what a thing is (ti esti) through prior and more intelligible terms without asserting its existence—e.g. defining a line as breadthless length.

kath-hauto.definition: An attribute belonging to a subject either inside its essential formula (as line in triangle) or containing the subject itself inside the attribute's own formula (as straight and curved belong to line).

katholou.definition: That which belongs to every instance (kata pantos), essentially (kath' hauto), and qua itself (hēi auto)—exemplified by the 2R angle-sum belonging commensurate-universally to triangle qua triangle rather than isosceles.

metabasis.loci: Anal. Post. I.7, 75a38–b20; De Caelo I.1, 268b1
metabasis.definition: Aristotle's structural law that an arithmetical proof cannot establish a geometrical theorem concerning continuous magnitudes unless the genera stand in formal subalternation (as optics to geometry).

to-hoti-kai-dioti.headword: τὸ ὅτι καὶ τὸ διότι (to hoti / to dioti)
to-hoti-kai-dioti.definition: Distinction between empirical sciences that know the fact (optics, harmonics, observational astronomy) and pure mathematical sciences that supply the formal geometrical or arithmetical reason why.

akribeia.definition: Precision proportional to conceptual simplicity and priority: arithmetic is more exact than geometry because the arithmetical monad lacks position, whereas the geometrical point adds position (thesis).

poson.definition: That which is divisible into constituent parts each capable of being a single determinate 'this'; the proper ontological domain of mathematics, bifurcated into discrete multitude and continuous magnitude.

diorismenon.definition: Quantity whose parts join at no common boundary (koinoi horoi), prototypically number (arithmos) and spoken logos.

syneches.definition: Quantity whose parts share a common boundary where their extremities become one, and which is divisible solely into parts that are themselves always further divisible (eis aei diaireta)—line, surface, body, time, and place.

adiaireton.loci: Phys. VI.1, 231a21–b18; De Anima III.6, 430b6–20; Metaph. Δ.6, 1016b24–31
adiaireton.definition: That which lacks parts in quantity or species; in geometry, the point is indivisible in every dimension yet possesses position, serving as limit (peras) of a line without ever composing it.

stigme.loci: Anal. Post. I.27, 87a36; Topics VI.4, 141b5–22; Phys. VI.1, 231a24–b18; Metaph. Δ.6, 1016b25
stigme.definition: Aristotle's standard term for the geometrical point (prior to Euclid's sēmeion): an indivisible substance having position (ousia athetos vs. thetos), functioning as boundary and division of continuous length.

monas.definition: That which is quantitatively indivisible in every respect and without spatial position (athetos), serving as the primary measure of discrete number.

megethos.definition: Measurable continuous quantity: divisible in one dimension as line (grammē), in two as plane surface (epipedon), and completely in three as solid body (sōma).

plethos.definition: Quantity countable into discontinuous parts; when limited and measured by the unit, multitude constitutes number (arithmos).

antanairesis.definition: The pre-Eudoxian definition of equality of ratios (preserved in Euclid Elements X.2–3): two magnitudes have the same ratio as two others when they undergo the exact same sequence of reciprocal subtractions.

asymmetron.loci: Anal. Prior. I.23, 41a23–30; Anal. Post. I.2, 71b26; Metaph. A.2, 983a15
asymmetron.definition: Aristotle'sparadigm of apodeictic necessity by reductio ad absurdum: if the diagonal of a square were commensurable with its side, odd numbers would become equal to even numbers.

chorismos.definition: The mathematician's legitimate methodological act of considering surfaces, volumes, lengths, and points apart from physical motion and sensible matter without asserting Platonic separate existence.

apeiron.definition: Not an actually completed magnitude (which is impossible), but an open-ended potentiality whereby another part can always be taken—inwardly by bisection in magnitudes, outwardly by succession in numbers.

topos.definition: The first motionless boundary of the containing body (to tou periechontos peras akinēton prōton, 212a20), grounding positional order without positing an empty self-subsistent void.

phantasia.definition: A movement generated by actual sense-perception that preserves spatial configuration and figure apart from external matter, bridging sensation (aisthēsis) and intellectual thought (noēsis).

phantasma.definition: The concrete imaginative presentation in which the intellect beholds universal formal structure; as the geometer draws a determinate finite triangle yet proves solely from its universal triangularity.

noesis.loci: Anal. Post. I.12, 77b30–31; De Anima III.4–8, 429a10–432a14
noesis.definition: Direct intellectual insight reading formal necessity inside mathematical constructions; highlighted by Hoenen as the Aristotelian text refuting blind symbolic formalism.

aphairesis.greek: τὰ ἐν ἀφαιρέσει / τὰ ἐξ ἀφαιρέσεως
aphairesis.loci: Anal. Post. I.18, 81b3; De Caelo III.1, 299a15; De Anima III.7, 431b12–17
aphairesis.definition: Aristotle's technical designation for mathematical entities obtained by stripping away sensible contraries (weight, heat, hardness) while retaining continuous quantitative determination.

hyle-noete.definition: Pure continuous spatial extension remaining after sensible qualities are abstracted; individuates multiple congruent circles or triangles that share the exact same formal definition.

energeia.definition: Priority of act over potency; in Metaphysics Θ.9 (1051a21–33), geometrical theorems are discovered by actualizing latent divisions through auxiliary lines, making the causal middle term immediately manifest.

dynamis.loci: Phys. III.6, 206a14–25; Metaph. Δ.12, 1019b33 (square in geometry); Θ.9, 1051a24
dynamis.definition: Both ontological potentiality (as latent chords and parallels exist potentially in a figure prior to construction, and infinite bisections exist potentially in a segment) and the technical Greek geometric term for a mathematical square.

entelecheia.loci: Phys. III.1, 201a10–11; De Anima II.1, 412a27; Metaph. Θ.8, 1050a21–23
entelecheia.definition: Aristotle's coinage signifying internal completeness or attainment of form (telos); used in Physics III.1 to define motion as the entelecheia of the potential qua potential.

to-ti-en-einai.headword: τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι (to ti ēn einai)
to-ti-en-einai.loci: Anal. Post. II.3–10; De Anima III.4, 429b10–22; Metaph. Z.4–11, 1029b1–1037b7
to-ti-en-einai.definition: What it is for a thing to be what it essentially is—e.g. 'to be straight' (to euthei einai) vs. the extended straight thing (to euthy) composed of form in continuum.

kalon.headword: τὸ καλόν — τάξις, συμμετρία, τὸ ὡρισμένον (to kalon)
kalon.definition: Aristotle's defence against Aristippus: mathematics pre-eminently exhibits the chief forms of beauty—order (taxis), symmetry/commensurability (symmetria), and determinate precision (to hōrismenon)—and acts as their causal explanation.

arithmos.translation: Discrete number (multitude measured by the unit)
arithmos.loci: Categoriae 6, 4b23–31; Phys. III.7, 207b7; Metaph. Δ.13, 1020a13; I.6, 1057a3
arithmos.definition: Limited multitude (plēthos peperasmenon) composed of indivisible units without spatial position; contrasted throughout Aristotle with continuous geometric magnitude (megethos).

aistheta-koina.translation: Common sensibles (movement, rest, number, figure, magnitude)
aistheta-koina.definition: Quantitative and kinematic determinations—movement, rest, number, figure (schēma), and magnitude (megethos)—perceived jointly across multiple senses (chiefly sight and touch) and retained in spatial phantasms.
